Set or get a model's calendar, for every year or for particular years

Source: R/class-config.R, R/calendar-years.R, R/geoscale.R
setCalendar.Rd

setCalendar() puts a calendar on a config, model or scenario; getCalendar() reads it back. With years, the calendar is given to those milestone years alone, and the model keeps its own for the rest.

Usage

# S4 method for class 'config'
setCalendar(obj, calendar = NULL, years = NULL, ...)

# S4 method for class 'model'
setCalendar(obj, calendar = NULL, years = NULL, ...)

# S4 method for class 'scenario'
setCalendar(obj, calendar = NULL, years = NULL, ...)

# S4 method for class 'config'
getCalendar(obj)

# S4 method for class 'model'
getCalendar(obj)

# S4 method for class 'scenario'
getCalendar(obj)

Arguments

obj

a config, settings, model or scenario.

calendar

a calendar object, or NULL to build one from ....

years

milestone years this calendar applies to, or NULL (default) to make it the model's calendar for every year.

...

passed to newCalendar() when calendar is not given.

Value

setCalendar() returns the modified object; getCalendar() returns a calendar.

Details

Pass a calendar object — an element of calendars, or one from newCalendar() or calendar_samples(). Leaving calendar out and giving newCalendar()'s arguments instead builds one on the spot, which is all this accepted up to version 0.92.

With years, the calendar is registered in config@misc$calendars and named on those rows of horizon@intervals, so a milestone can be solved on a sample of the model calendar: hourly where the investment decisions land, cheaper in the years that only carry the trajectory forward.

Such a calendar must be a sample rather than a different calendar — the same timeframe levels, slices drawn from the model calendar's own universe, the same share for a slice the two share. What may differ is which slices a year has and how many times each stands for (its weight). The check runs here, where the call that broke it can be named: dropping a level instead of sampling its members re-derives the leaf timeslice names and the year would then solve to zero in silence.

See also

getYearCalendars(), calendar_samples(), calendars

Examples

# milestones 2030, 2035 and 2040: `period` is a span, so it is given in
# full and the interval widths carve it up
mod <- newModel("demo", calendar = calendars$d365_h24,
                horizon = newHorizon(2030:2040, intervals = c(1, 5, 5),
                                     mid_is_end = TRUE))
getCalendar(mod)@name
#> [1] "d365_h24"

# 2035 on one day per month, the other two years hourly
mod <- setCalendar(mod, calendars$d365_h24_1dpm, years = 2035)
names(getYearCalendars(mod))
#> [1] "2030" "2035" "2040"
mod@config@horizon@intervals$calendar
#> [1] NA              "d365_h24_1dpm" NA
